name: Grillz

image.caption: Top and bottom custom grillz 14k gold

lead: Grillz are decorative covers, usually gold, silver or platinum and sometimes set with stones, worn over some or all of the teeth. They are jewelry for the mouth and a fashion signature in hip-hop culture.

They help looks by turning the smile into an accessory and signalling style or status. Wikipedia traces the modern trend to New York in the early 1980s and to Southern rap in the 2000s, with Nelly's 2005 song "Grillz" a notable pop-culture moment.

paras: Custom grillz are cast from a dental mold and worn over the teeth, then removed for eating and cleaning; cheaper stock versions use generic shapes. Wearers typically choose metal, number of teeth and stones.

Wikipedia reports the American Dental Association has said there is no conclusive safety research; base metals can cause irritation or allergy, and long-term wear can trap bacteria linked to gum disease and cavities. Some jewelers making grills from impressions have faced charges for unlicensed dentistry.

angle.text: Grillz change the look of the smile into a piece of jewelry. Wearers pick metal, colour and stones to match their personal style.

lead: Grillz, also written grills, are metal ornaments worn over the teeth, commonly gold, silver or platinum and sometimes set with gemstones.[1] They are also called fronts or golds.[1]

Tooth decoration dates back thousands of years, but modern grills spread from New York in the early 1980s and then through Atlanta and Miami, becoming a national trend with the rise of Southern rap in the 2000s.[1] Wearers have included rappers such as Paul Wall and mainstream stars.[1]

Dental publications in 2006 discussed grills for patients and whether making them could count as practising dentistry.[2][3] An academic paper in 2022 analysed grills as an artefact that reshapes the face and identity.[4]

paras: Higher-end grills are made from a dental mold, cast in gold, finished by hand and sometimes set with stones; cheaper ones use generic shapes and base metals such as brass or nickel.[1] Gold ranges from 10 to 24 karat in several colours.[1]

The style grew from 1980s New York hip hop and spread south, and later appeared in music such as Nelly's 2005 single "Grillz".[1][5] Some school districts in Alabama, Georgia and Texas have banned them.[1]

The American Dental Association has said conclusive safety research is lacking; occasional well-fitting wear carries low risk, while base metals can irritate and long-term wear can trap bacteria.[1] Dental editorials from 2006 addressed the same concerns.[2][3]

timeline.event: Gold tooth caps become popular with New York hip-hop artists.[1]
